endo00: An endoleak is blood still flowing into an aneurysm sac after endovascular repair.
endo01: Type one is a leak at the seal zones, at the top or at the iliac limbs. It's high pressure, and needs prompt repair.
endo02: Type two is the most common. Blood flows backwards into the sac from a lumbar artery or the inferior mesenteric artery.
endo03: Many seal on their own, and are treated only if the sac keeps growing.
endo04: Type three is a tear in the graft, or a separation between its parts. Also high pressure, and fixed promptly.
endo05: Type four is seepage through the porous graft fabric soon after placement. It resolves on its own.
endo06: Type five, or endotension, is a growing sac with no visible leak.
endo07: On C-T angiography, look for contrast inside the sac but outside the graft, on arterial and delayed phases.
endo08: Types one and three are the urgent ones.
budd00: Budd kee-AR-ee syndrome is blocked outflow from the liver, anywhere from the hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava.
budd01: Causes include myeloproliferative disorders, other clotting disorders, the oral contraceptive pill, and a membrane in the I-V-C.
budd02: Patients present with abdominal pain, a large liver, and ascites.
budd03: On Doppler, the hepatic veins are clotted, absent, or have flat or reversed flow.
budd04: The caudate lobe enlarges, because it drains straight into the I-V-C through its own small veins.
budd05: On contrast C-T, the centre of the liver enhances more than the periphery, giving a patchy, mosaic pattern.
budd06: Treatment ranges from anticoagulation, to angioplasty, a tips, or a liver transplant.
budd07: Ascites, a big caudate, and no hepatic veins? Think Budd kee-AR-ee.
